Adorno's writing on jazz, which he treated as a paradigm case of standardised pseudo-freedom, is widely regarded as ignorant of the music and coloured by a European high-cultural disdain that shades into something worse given jazz's African-American origins. The theory also cannot easily explain the failure of most cultural products, the emergence of genuinely subversive work from within commercial systems, or the fragmentation of audiences. Adorno partially revisited the argument in a 1963 essay, conceding some points and conceding little of the substance.

sections.heading: Adorno: Negative Dialectics and the Defence of Art
sections.body:
Theodor Adorno (1903-1969) is the tradition's most difficult and most original figure, and his mature philosophy is an attempt to think without doing violence to what is thought about.

Negative Dialectics (1966) is the statement of it. Adorno's target is what he calls identity thinking: the ordinary operation of subsuming a particular under a general concept, saying that this thing is an instance of that kind. He argues that this operation, indispensable as it is, always leaves a remainder. The concept never exhausts the object; something particular is always suppressed. Adorno takes this logical point and gives it a social content, arguing that the same structure appears in exchange, where qualitatively different labours and goods are equated by reduction to a common measure, and in administration, where individuals become cases. Identity thinking is not merely an error of philosophers; it is the intellectual form of a society that reduces everything to equivalence.

His alternative is not to abandon concepts, which would be impossible, but to use them against themselves — to arrange them into what he calls constellations that circle an object and illuminate it without pretending to capture it. Hence "negative" dialectics: unlike Hegel's, it does not resolve contradictions into a higher synthesis, and it refuses the consolation of a positive result. This is why Adorno's prose is so demanding. He believed that a smooth, systematic, easily digestible presentation would itself enact the reduction he was arguing against, and he wrote accordingly, in dense paratactic sentences that resist summary. Whether that is intellectual integrity or a failure of communication is a fair question, and it has been asked by sympathetic readers as well as hostile ones.

Art occupies the crucial place in his thought, and his posthumously published Aesthetic Theory (1970) is the fullest account. Adorno held that authentic modernist art — Schoenberg's atonal music, Beckett's plays, Kafka's fiction — preserves a trace of what the administered world excludes. It does so not by delivering political messages, which he regarded as a betrayal of art's medium, but formally: by refusing to be pleasant, by refusing resolution, by making its own difficulty a protest against a culture of easy consumption. The dissonance that will not resolve is a truth-content about a world whose contradictions are not resolved either.

This position generated the tradition's sharpest internal argument. Walter Benjamin and Bertolt Brecht both held that art should intervene politically and that new technologies of reproduction opened democratic possibilities; Adorno thought this collapsed art into propaganda and overestimated the technology. The exchange of letters between Adorno and Benjamin in the late 1930s is among the most illuminating documents in twentieth-century aesthetics, and neither man persuaded the other.

sections.heading: Marcuse: One-Dimensional Man and the New Left
sections.body:
Herbert Marcuse (1898-1979) was the member of the school who became genuinely famous, and the only one who became a political figure. Having remained in the United States after the war, teaching at Brandeis and then at the University of California, San Diego, he wrote in English for an American audience and reached a readership the others never did.

Eros and Civilization (1955) was his attempt to turn Freud against Freud. Freud had argued in Civilization and Its Discontents that civilisation necessarily requires the repression of instinctual drives, because the work of survival demands that pleasure be deferred. Marcuse accepted the structure but introduced a distinction: some repression is genuinely necessary given scarcity, but a further quantity, which he called surplus repression, exists only to sustain particular relations of domination. His claim was that advanced industrial productivity had largely abolished the material scarcity that justified the basic repression, so that most of what remained was surplus, and that a non-repressive civilisation with a transformed, eroticised relation to work and the body was technically possible. This argument, more than any other single text, connected Frankfurt theory to the counterculture of the 1960s.

One-Dimensional Man (1964) is his major and bleakest work. Its thesis is that advanced industrial society has achieved something no previous system managed: it has absorbed and neutralised opposition, not by repression but by delivery. It gives people goods, comfort, entertainment and rising living standards, and in doing so produces what Marcuse called false needs — wants generated by the system whose satisfaction binds the individual more tightly to it. Political language flattens; alternatives become literally unthinkable because the vocabulary for imagining them has been eroded. Even dissent is absorbed and marketed. The result is a "one-dimensional" society with no negative pole, no outside from which critique can be launched, and a comfortable, smooth unfreedom. Marcuse's tentative hope lay with those outside the system's benefits: the unemployed, racial minorities, students, the populations of the developing world.

His 1965 essay "Repressive Tolerance" is his most contested and remains genuinely controversial. Marcuse argued that formal, neutral tolerance in a society of unequal power functions to preserve that inequality, since all views get an equal hearing but only some have amplification; he concluded that tolerance in such conditions is repressive and advocated what he called liberating tolerance, involving withdrawal of tolerance from movements of the right. Critics across the political spectrum, including liberals sympathetic to his other work, regard this as a straightforward argument for censorship and a serious failure of nerve about free speech. It is regularly cited in contemporary debates about deplatforming, usually by opponents. Marcuse became a public target in the United States, received death threats, and was for a period the most notorious philosopher in America.

sections.heading: Benjamin: The Outsider Who Became Central
sections.body:
Walter Benjamin (1892-1940) was never a salaried member of the Institute, and his relationship with it was uneasy — dependent on its stipends, edited and sometimes rejected by Adorno, personally isolated. He is now, by a wide margin, its most widely read associate, and his influence extends into media studies, art history, literary criticism and photography theory.

His most cited essay, "The Work of Art in the Age of Its Technological Reproducibility", exists in several versions written between 1935 and 1939. Its central concept is aura: the unique presence of an artwork in a particular place and time, its embeddedness in tradition and ritual, the quality that makes standing before an original painting different from seeing a reproduction. Benjamin argued that technologies of mass reproduction — photography above all, then film — destroy aura, and that this destruction is genuinely ambivalent. Something is lost: the work's authority, its distance, its rootedness. But something is gained: the work is detached from ritual, brought close to the masses, and made available for political rather than cultic use. Film in particular, with its montage and its shock effects, trains a new kind of distracted, collective, critical perception.

The essay's closing move is its most quoted: fascism, Benjamin wrote, responds to the masses' demand for change by giving them expression without altering property relations, which amounts to an aestheticisation of politics culminating in war; communism, he answered, responds by politicising art. Whether this is a profound diagnosis or a slogan is arguable, but the phrase "aestheticisation of politics" has proved durable.

Benjamin's other major projects were the unfinished Arcades Project, a vast montage of quotations and commentary on nineteenth-century Paris intended as a prehistory of modernity read through its commodity spaces, and the late "On the Concept of History", eighteen theses written in 1940. The ninth thesis, describing Paul Klee's monoprint Angelus Novus as an angel blown backwards into the future by a storm called progress while the wreckage of history piles up before it, is among the most famous images in modern thought. The theses attack the idea of history as smooth progress, insist that every document of civilisation is also a document of barbarism, and combine Marxist and Jewish messianic vocabulary in ways scholars still argue about.

Benjamin's own death gives the work an unbearable frame. Fleeing occupied France in September 1940, he crossed the Pyrenees on foot to Portbou on the Spanish border, was told the group would be returned to France, and took a fatal dose of morphine that night. Those travelling with him were permitted to continue the following day. He was 48.

His relationship to the school's other members remains contested by scholars. Adorno championed him and also constrained him, rejecting a version of an Arcades-related essay in 1938 on the grounds that its juxtaposition of economic detail and cultural fragment lacked mediating theory — an editorial judgement that Benjamin's later admirers have often read as an act of intellectual suppression, and that Adorno's defenders read as sound criticism honestly given. What is not in dispute is that Benjamin's method, which builds an argument out of assembled fragments and concrete particulars rather than out of a system, is genuinely his own, and that it has proved far more portable to other disciplines than anything else the circle produced.

sections.heading: Return to Frankfurt, Public Life, and the Break of 1968
sections.body:
Horkheimer and Adorno returned to West Germany in 1949 and 1950, and the Institute reopened in Frankfurt in 1951 in a new building. It was funded partly by the city and partly by American occupation authorities interested in democratic re-education, which is a considerable irony for a group that had spent the previous decade dissecting American mass culture.

The postwar Institute did substantial empirical work. The Group Experiment, conducted in 1950-51 and published in 1955, used recorded group discussions rather than questionnaires to probe what Germans actually said among themselves about guilt, the Nazi period and Jews, and its findings — widespread defensiveness, resentment and evasion beneath a surface of official contrition — were unwelcome. Friedrich Pollock's earlier thesis about state capitalism also shaped the Institute's postwar economics: Pollock had argued in 1941 that both Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union represented a new formation in which the political administration, not the market, had become the primary allocator, and that this dissolved the classical Marxist expectation that economic crisis would generate political change. Franz Neumann had disagreed sharply, insisting in Behemoth that Nazi Germany remained recognisably capitalist. The unresolved argument is one reason the tradition's later economics is so thin.

Adorno became, unexpectedly, a major German public intellectual, delivering radio talks and lectures on education, memory and democracy. Two are still widely read: "What Does Coming to Terms with the Past Mean?" (1959), which argued that Germany's official reckoning risked becoming a way of closing the subject rather than confronting it, and "Education After Auschwitz" (1966), which opens with the claim that the premier demand on all education is that Auschwitz not happen again. These are among his clearest and most humane writings, and they complicate the picture of a purely pessimistic mandarin.

Then came 1968, and it broke the school. The German student movement, radicalised by the shooting of the student Benno Ohnesorg by a police officer in June 1967 and the attempted assassination of Rudi Dutschke in April 1968, read Marcuse and Adorno as authorising revolutionary action. Adorno would not endorse it. He regarded the students' actionism as pseudo-activity that substituted gesture for thought, and he feared it would provoke reaction rather than change. In January 1969, when students occupied the Institute, he called the police, and 76 people were arrested. In April, three women students disrupted his lecture in a mocking protest that the press dubbed the "breast attack". His correspondence with Marcuse that spring is painful reading: Marcuse, sympathetic to the students, told him bluntly that they were doing what his own theory implied, and Adorno replied that a theory which produced barricades had misunderstood itself.

Adorno died of a heart attack in Switzerland on 6 August 1969, aged 65, exhausted and publicly attacked from the left. Horkheimer died in 1973. The first generation ended without resolving the question of what critical theory was supposed to do.

sections.heading: Habermas and the Communicative Turn
sections.body:
Jürgen Habermas, born in 1929 and Adorno's research assistant in the late 1950s, rebuilt the tradition on entirely different foundations, and his work is the reason critical theory survived as a live research programme rather than becoming a chapter in intellectual history.

His diagnosis of his teachers was blunt. Dialectic of Enlightenment, he argued, had painted itself into a corner: by identifying reason as such with instrumental, means-ends calculation, it left itself no rational standpoint from which to criticise anything, so that its own critique became a performative contradiction — an act of reasoning that denies reason's competence. Habermas's solution was to deny the premise. Instrumental reason, he argued, is not the whole of reason; it is one type. Alongside it stands communicative reason, the kind exercised whenever people try to reach genuine understanding with one another rather than merely to influence one another.

The analysis rests on a claim about language. Whenever a speaker makes a serious assertion, Habermas argues, they implicitly raise validity claims that can be challenged and defended with reasons: that the statement is true, that it is normatively right in the context, and that the speaker is being sincere, with comprehensibility as a background condition. Communication oriented to understanding therefore has built into it an orientation toward reasoned agreement. From this he derives a counterfactual standard, the ideal speech situation, in which all affected parties participate, all may question any assertion, and no force operates except that of the better argument. Real discourse never meets this standard, but it is presupposed by the practice of arguing, and it supplies the normative benchmark the first generation lacked.

The Theory of Communicative Action, published in two volumes in 1981, applies this at the level of society through the distinction between lifeworld and system. The lifeworld is the shared background of meanings, norms and solidarities reproduced through communication: family, culture, public opinion. The system comprises the domains coordinated by the non-linguistic media of money and power: the economy and the state bureaucracy. Both are necessary, and the differentiation of system from lifeworld is a genuine achievement of modernity. The pathology Habermas identifies is colonisation of the lifeworld — the encroachment of money and administrative power into domains that can only be reproduced communicatively, so that education, care, culture and civic life are progressively reorganised as markets and as administrative procedures. This is a considerably more precise and more testable claim than "the administered society", and it names losses without condemning modernity as such.

His earlier Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962) had traced the rise of a bourgeois public sphere in the coffee houses, salons and periodicals of the eighteenth century and its subsequent decay into managed publicity. Between Facts and Norms (1992) developed a deliberative theory of democracy and law in which legitimacy derives from procedures that give citizens genuine communicative influence. Habermas also became one of Europe's most prominent public intellectuals, arguing against postmodernism, defending the Enlightenment as an unfinished project, and writing at length on European integration and on religion in a post-secular society.

sections.heading: Recognition, Justice, and Critical Theory Today
sections.body:
The third generation is dominated by Axel Honneth, born in 1949, who studied with Habermas and directed the Institute for Social Research from 2001 to 2018. His central move was to relocate the normative foundations of critical theory from language to recognition.

The Struggle for Recognition (1992) draws on Hegel's early Jena writings and on the American social psychologist George Herbert Mead to argue that human beings become selves only through being recognised by others, and that recognition takes three distinct forms, each supporting a different dimension of a functioning self-relation. Love and friendship, in the sphere of intimate relations, produce basic self-confidence: the sense that one's needs matter. Legal recognition, in the sphere of rights, produces self-respect: the sense of oneself as a person with equal standing. Esteem, in the sphere of solidarity and shared values, produces self-esteem: the sense that one's particular abilities and contributions have worth.

The critical payoff is that each form has a corresponding injury — abuse and violation, denial of rights, denigration of a way of life — and Honneth argues that experiences of disrespect are the moral motor of social conflict. Struggles that look like conflicts over resources are frequently, at their root, demands to be recognised. This gives critical theory a normative standard grounded in the conditions of human self-realisation, and a way of reading actual social movements as bearing moral content rather than needing to be told what their interests are.

The most important argument about this came from Nancy Fraser, whose exchange with Honneth was published in 2003 as Redistribution or Recognition? Fraser's objection is that recognition cannot absorb distribution. Some injustices are economic in origin and are not remedied by respect: a low-paid worker who is fully esteemed remains low-paid. She proposes instead a perspectival dualism that treats maldistribution and misrecognition as analytically distinct and equally fundamental, and she had earlier argued, in a 1985 essay, that Habermas's system-lifeworld distinction was gender-blind, since it classified the family as a lifeworld institution while ignoring the power and unpaid labour running through it. The Fraser-Honneth exchange is the clearest entry point into contemporary critical theory's central disagreement.

Other contemporary work has widened the field considerably. Rainer Forst grounds critique in a basic right to justification: nobody may be subjected to arrangements for which no adequate reasons can be given to them. Rahel Jaeggi has revived the concept of alienation and defended the possibility of criticising whole forms of life. Hartmut Rosa has developed a theory of social acceleration and its counterpart, resonance, arguing that modern society stabilises itself only by continual growth and speed-up. Amy Allen has pressed the tradition hard on its residual assumptions of historical progress and its Eurocentrism, arguing that a critical theory serious about colonialism cannot rest on a story of Western moral learning. The field is now genuinely plural, and it is no longer confined to Frankfurt or to German.

sections.heading: Criticisms, Confusions, and How to Read the Tradition
sections.body:
The tradition attracts serious objections, and taking them seriously is part of understanding it.

The oldest is the charge of obscurantism and unfalsifiability, pressed by Karl Popper in the so-called positivism dispute that began with a 1961 conference at Tübingen where Popper and Adorno presented papers on the logic of the social sciences. Popper's position was that social science proceeds, like all science, by conjecture and attempted refutation, and that critical theory's central claims were framed so that no observation could count against them. Adorno's reply, that the demand for falsifiable propositions already presupposes the reified conception of facts under examination, is either a deep response or a refusal to answer, and readers divide on this to the present day. The related complaint about prose is harder to defend against: even sympathetic scholars concede that Adorno is often gratuitously difficult.

The second charge is political futility. Georg Lukács, in a 1962 preface, described the German intelligentsia as taking up residence in the "Grand Hotel Abyss", a comfortable establishment on the edge of nothingness where the contemplation of the void was enjoyed between excellent meals — an image aimed squarely at Adorno, and the source of the title of Stuart Jeffries's 2016 popular history. The point has force: a tradition committed in principle to the unity of theory and emancipatory practice produced, over half a century, almost no practice.

The third is empirical. The passive-audience assumption underlying the culture industry thesis has been substantially undermined by media research, particularly Stuart Hall's 1973 encoding-decoding model and the ethnographic audience studies that followed, which found people routinely producing oppositional readings of the products supposedly programming them. The Authoritarian Personality's instruments were methodologically weak. And the school's near-silence on colonialism and race, at a time when European empires still governed much of the world, is a significant gap that postcolonial critics and, from within the tradition, Amy Allen have pressed.

A separate matter needs stating plainly because it dominates online discussion. Since the 1990s a conspiracy theory has circulated claiming that the Frankfurt School deliberately set out to destroy Western civilisation by subverting its culture, usually under the label "cultural Marxism". It was propagated in a 1992 article by Michael Minnicino associated with the Lyndon LaRouche movement and subsequently by the American writer William Lind, and it reproduces the structure and much of the content of the Nazi propaganda charge of Kulturbolschewismus, including its focus on Jewish intellectuals. Historians of the school, including Martin Jay, whose 1973 study The Dialectical Imagination remains the standard history, have documented this lineage in detail. It is possible to think the Frankfurt School wrong about almost everything, as many serious scholars do, without adopting a conspiracy narrative that misrepresents what its members argued and why.

For a reader beginning now, the practical advice is to start with the accessible texts rather than the famous ones: Adorno's "Education After Auschwitz", Benjamin's essay on reproducibility, Marcuse's introduction to One-Dimensional Man. Read Dialectic of Enlightenment later, slowly, and read a good history alongside it — Jay's, or Rolf Wiggershaus's fuller 1986 account.

guides.title: Social Constructionism
guides.summary: What it means to say something is socially constructed: the intellectual history from Vico and Durkheim through Berger and Luckmann to Foucault, Searle and Hacking, the major case studies of race, gender and mental illness, and the serious objections the position has to answer.

sections.heading: What the Claim Actually Says
sections.body:
To say that something is socially constructed is to say that it exists because of human collective activity rather than independently of it, and that it could have been otherwise. The phrase is used so widely, and so often as a weapon, that its precise content has become blurred. Recovering that content is worth doing carefully, because in its disciplined form the idea is one of the more powerful analytical tools the social sciences have produced, and in its careless form it is a way of dismissing anything inconvenient.

Begin with a clear example. A twenty-pound note is a rectangle of polymer with ink on it. Its physical properties — mass, tensile strength, spectral reflectance — exist whether or not anyone believes in them. Its property of being worth twenty pounds does not. That property exists because a very large number of people, most of whom will never meet, collectively treat the object as having it, and because institutions such as a central bank, a legal system and a banking network sustain that treatment. If everyone stopped accepting it tomorrow, the note would cease to be money while remaining physically unchanged. Money is therefore socially constructed in a strict and uncontroversial sense.

Two things follow that are constantly misunderstood. First, socially constructed does not mean unreal. The value of that note is entirely real: it will get you a meal, and a court will treat theft of it as theft of twenty pounds. Constructed things have causes and effects, and often the most powerful effects in a person's life — marriage, citizenship, debt, criminal conviction — are constructed ones. Second, socially constructed does not mean arbitrary, optional or easy to change. Constructions are held in place by institutions, laws, habits, material infrastructure and the beliefs of millions of people. National borders are constructed and are also defended by armies.

The genuinely contested question is not whether money or borders are constructed but how far the analysis extends. Is race constructed? Gender? Mental illness? Childhood? Emotions? The categories of natural science? Each of these has been claimed, and each claim means something different and carries a different burden of proof. A large part of the value of the field lies in learning to ask, of any particular claim, exactly what is supposed to have been constructed, by whom, out of what materials, and with what consequences.

The philosopher Ian Hacking observed that construction talk usually carries an implicit political charge beyond the descriptive claim: it suggests that the thing in question was not inevitable, and often that we would be better off without it. Separating the descriptive claim from that evaluative one is the first discipline the subject requires, because the descriptive claim can be true while the evaluative one is false, and the two are routinely bundled together.

sections.heading: Brute Facts and Institutional Facts
sections.body:
The cleanest framework for keeping construction talk honest was set out by the philosopher John Searle in The Construction of Social Reality in 1995, and it is useful even to people who disagree with his broader philosophy. Searle distinguishes brute facts from institutional facts. A brute fact holds independently of any human institution: that a particular mountain is 4,478 metres high, that hydrogen has one proton, that a certain object weighs 3 kilograms. An institutional fact holds only because of a human institution: that the mountain lies in Switzerland, that this piece of plastic is a driving licence, that these two people are married.

Institutional facts are created, on Searle's account, by constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in context C". A bordered rectangle of paper issued by the Bank of England counts as legal tender in the United Kingdom. Making certain marks on a certain form in front of certain witnesses counts as entering a marriage in this jurisdiction. Crossing the goal line with the ball counts as a try in rugby. These rules do not regulate an activity that could exist without them, as a speed limit regulates driving; they bring the activity into existence. Chess is not a game that existed and then acquired rules. The rules are what make the moves moves.

Two further ingredients are needed. The first is what Searle calls collective intentionality: the capacity of people to intend and believe things together, in the form "we accept that this counts as that", which he argues is not reducible to a sum of individual intentions. The second is the status function: the object acquires a function it could not perform through its physical properties alone. A wall keeps people out by being physically hard, which is not a status function. A line of stones on a border keeps people out by being recognised as a boundary, which is.

Crucially, Searle holds that institutional facts require a background of brute facts. Money requires something physical, or at least a physical record, to bear the status. Language requires sounds or marks. Institutions are layered on reality; they do not float. Searle is an unapologetic external realist who wrote the book partly to show that acknowledging a vast domain of socially constructed reality is entirely compatible with, and indeed depends on, there being a mind-independent world.

This framework does real work. It lets you ask, of any construction claim, what the X and the Y are, who the "we" is that does the accepting, and what happens at the edges when the acceptance is contested. Applied to money, it explains inflation crises and currency collapses. Applied to race, it forces the question of exactly which status is being assigned to which physical facts, and by which institutions — a question that turns out to have historically specific and revealing answers.

sections.heading: The Ancestry: Vico, Kant, Marx, Durkheim
sections.body:
The idea did not arrive fully formed in the twentieth century. Its earliest clear statement belongs to the Neapolitan philosopher Giambattista Vico, whose New Science of 1725 advanced the principle verum ipsum factum — the true and the made are convertible. Vico argued that we can have genuine knowledge of history, law, language and myth in a way we cannot have of nature, precisely because human beings made the former and God made the latter. That inversion of the usual hierarchy, placing the human sciences on firmer epistemic ground than physics, is the ancestor of every later claim that social reality is our own product.

Immanuel Kant supplied a different half of the inheritance. In the Critique of Pure Reason of 1781 he argued that the mind does not passively receive the world but actively organises it: space, time and the categories such as causality are contributions of the knowing subject, so that we experience appearances structured by our own faculties rather than things as they are in themselves. Kant's structuring apparatus was universal and individual rather than historical and social, but the move — from a world simply given to a world partly constituted by the knower — is the one that later thinkers socialised. Replace Kant's fixed transcendental categories with historically varying social ones and you have much of the modern position.

Karl Marx made the categories social and historical. His 1859 preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy states the thesis compactly: it is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but their social being that determines their consciousness. In Capital he analysed the commodity fetish, whereby relations between people take on the appearance of relations between things and the historically specific arrangements of capitalism come to seem natural and inevitable. The idea that an apparently natural order is in fact a made one whose madeness has been forgotten is the animating impulse of much later constructionist work.

Émile Durkheim gave the position its sociological form. In The Rules of Sociological Method of 1895 he defined the social fact as a way of acting, thinking and feeling that is external to the individual and endowed with coercive power, and insisted that social facts be treated as things, explicable by other social facts rather than by psychology. In The Elementary Forms of Religious Life of 1912 he went further, arguing that even the fundamental categories of thought — time, space, class, causality — originate in social organisation, so that religion is in a real sense society worshipping itself.

Karl Mannheim consolidated this into a programme. His Ideology and Utopia of 1929 established the sociology of knowledge as the study of how thought is conditioned by social position, and raised the problem that has haunted the field since: if all thought is socially conditioned, what is the status of that claim itself?

sections.heading: Berger and Luckmann and the Founding Text
sections.body:
The phrase that names the field comes from a single book: The Social Construction of Reality: A Treatise in the Sociology of Knowledge, published in 1966 by Peter L. Berger and Thomas Luckmann. Both were students of the Austrian phenomenologist Alfred Schütz, and their project was to redirect the sociology of knowledge away from the study of grand ideologies and theories, which is what Mannheim had made it, toward the far larger and more consequential domain of everyday common-sense knowledge — what ordinary people take for granted as simply how things are.

Their argument turns on a three-part dialectic, stated in three propositions that must be held together: society is a human product; society is an objective reality; the human being is a social product. Each proposition corresponds to a moment in a continuous process. Externalisation is the outpouring of human activity into the world, in speech, work, institutions and artefacts. Objectivation is the moment at which those products acquire a facticity that confronts their makers as something external and given, as though they had always been there. Internalisation is the process by which the next generation takes that objective world into itself through socialisation, so that it becomes their subjective reality too.

The crucial and often-missed point is that the second moment involves a kind of forgetting, which Berger and Luckmann call reification: treating human products as if they were facts of nature, or the results of cosmic law, or manifestations of divine will. The reified world is experienced as strange and overwhelming rather than as one's own work. A person may say that they cannot leave their job because that is simply how the world is, or that a caste position is ordained, and in saying so they mistake a human arrangement for a natural necessity. Sociology's critical value, on this account, lies in recovering the human authorship of the social world without pretending that it can therefore be changed at will.

Their treatment of socialisation is equally careful. Primary socialisation, in childhood, is not a matter of learning information but of acquiring a world along with the emotionally charged relationships to the significant others who transmit it, which is why the reality laid down then is so difficult to dislodge. Secondary socialisation, into occupations and specialised roles, is thinner, more easily detached, and can be undone. Where a person must abandon one reality for another, as in religious conversion or in the total institutions Erving Goffman studied, Berger and Luckmann speak of alternation, which requires an intense plausibility structure — a community of others who confirm the new reality — to succeed.

The book has been criticised for saying little about power and inequality, a gap that Foucault and later feminist and postcolonial scholarship filled. But its core account of how the made becomes the given remains the field's foundation.

sections.heading: Language, Typification and Sedimented Knowledge
sections.body:
The mechanism by which a shared social reality is built and transmitted is, on almost every version of the theory, language. Alfred Schütz's phenomenology, which Berger and Luckmann adapted, describes ordinary consciousness as operating in the natural attitude, a stance in which the world is simply taken as there, shared with others, and available for practical purposes without being questioned. Within that attitude, we do not encounter unique particulars. We encounter types.

Typification is the process of apprehending something not in its individuality but as an instance of a kind: a bus, a customer, a headache, a policeman. Types come to us pre-packaged in language, and they carry with them a recipe for how to act. Recognising a person as a shop assistant tells you what to expect, what is permitted, what would be strange. Schütz observed that most social interaction proceeds through such anonymous typifications, becoming more concrete only for the people we know well. The stock of typifications a society possesses is its common-sense knowledge, and it is unevenly distributed: what counts as obvious to a farmer, a lawyer or a nurse differs, and the sociology of knowledge studies precisely this distribution.

Language does more than label. Because it can refer to what is absent, past, hypothetical or impossible, language detaches meaning from the here and now and allows the construction of vast symbolic universes — religion, law, science, national history — that integrate all the smaller meanings into a single order and locate an individual life within it. These universes require maintenance. When they are challenged, societies generate what Berger and Luckmann call universe-maintaining machinery: theology, mythology, philosophy, and in modern conditions the professions and the sciences, along with therapy for those who deviate and nihilation, the strategy of explaining away rival realities as ignorance, madness or bad faith.

Sedimentation is the term for how experience becomes shared knowledge. Individual experiences that are remembered congeal into recognisable forms; those retained by more than one person become intersubjective; those encoded in a sign system, above all in writing, become detachable from anyone's biography and transmissible to people who never had the original experience. A body of law, a medical textbook or a national curriculum is sedimented experience, and by the time it reaches a student it arrives as objective fact rather than as somebody's accumulated interpretation.

This account explains an important asymmetry. A newborn confronts a social world already fully formed, with names for everything, expected behaviours, and sanctions for departures. From the inside, that world does not feel constructed at all; it feels like the way things are. The theoretical claim is not that people experience their world as made — they emphatically do not — but that an analyst can trace the historical process by which it came to be, and can therefore recover the possibility that it might have been otherwise.

sections.heading: Institutions, Habitualisation and Legitimation
sections.body:
Constructionism becomes concrete when it explains how institutions form, and the account given in 1966 remains serviceable. It begins with habitualisation. Any action repeated frequently settles into a pattern that can be reproduced with economy of effort, and this is true even of a solitary person: a castaway alone on an island develops routines. Habitualisation narrows choice, which is a benefit, since a being who had to deliberate afresh about every action could not function. It provides a stable background against which deliberation about genuinely novel problems becomes possible.

Institutionalisation occurs when habitualised actions are reciprocally typified by types of actors — when it is understood that actions of this kind are performed by people of that kind. Two people who improvise a division of labour have not yet created an institution; they know they invented it and could change it. The decisive transition comes with a third party who was not present at the founding, above all with children. To the new generation the arrangement is not a negotiated convention but simply the way things are done, an objective fact of the world confronted as external and coercive. The institution has acquired a history, and history is what gives it its objectivity.

Because institutions control conduct by setting up predefined patterns and channelling behaviour away from alternatives, they need mechanisms of social control only where the primary control of habit and expectation fails. And because they must be transmitted to people who did not create them, they require legitimation: an explanation and justification of why things are as they are. Berger and Luckmann describe four ascending levels. The first is linguistic, present as soon as a vocabulary exists — calling a relative a cousin already carries obligations. The second is rudimentary theoretical propositions in the form of proverbs, maxims and folk tales. The third is explicit theory administered by specialists. The fourth is the symbolic universe, an integrating framework such as a religion or a nationalism that places the whole social order within a cosmology.

Two consequences deserve emphasis. First, institutions tend toward integration not because they were designed as a coherent system but because the people who live within several of them at once are one person, and so must reconcile them; the appearance of systematic coherence is largely a retrospective achievement of legitimating theory. Second, roles do the work of connecting the individual to the institutional order. To play a role is to represent an institution: a judge on the bench is not merely a person with opinions but the embodiment of a legal order, and the role carries knowledge that the person must acquire.

This is why constructed institutions are hard rather than soft. Habit, socialisation, sanction, legitimation and material infrastructure all hold them in place, which is exactly why deliberate reform so often disappoints.

sections.heading: Symbolic Interactionism and the Thomas Theorem
sections.body:
A parallel American tradition arrived at overlapping conclusions from a different direction, and it supplies the field's most quoted single sentence. In 1928, in The Child in America, William Isaac Thomas and Dorothy Swaine Thomas wrote that if men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences. The Thomas theorem does not say that belief makes things true. It says that people act on their definitions of a situation, and those actions have effects that are entirely real regardless of whether the original definition was accurate.

Robert K. Merton turned this into the self-fulfilling prophecy in a 1948 essay, with the example of a solvent bank that fails because a false rumour of insolvency prompts a run. The bank's insolvency was not a fact until the belief in it produced the behaviour that made it one. The mechanism generalises: a teacher who believes a pupil is able attends to that pupil differently and may produce the ability; a stereotype about a group can shape the behaviour of both the stereotyped and everyone else until confirming evidence accumulates. This is a causal pathway by which classifications remake the world they claim only to describe.

The wider tradition, named symbolic interactionism by Herbert Blumer in 1937, drew on George Herbert Mead, whose lectures were published posthumously in 1934 as Mind, Self, and Society. Mead argued that the self is not a precondition of social life but a product of it: the child acquires a self by learning to take the attitude of others toward itself, first of particular significant others in play, then of an organised community of others — the generalised other — in games with rules. Mead distinguished the spontaneous, acting I from the socially reflected me. On this account even the innermost sense of being a person is socially produced.

Blumer set out three premises in 1969: people act toward things on the basis of the meanings those things have for them; meanings arise out of social interaction; and meanings are handled and modified through an interpretive process. The third premise is a real corrective to more deterministic accounts, since it makes people active interpreters rather than passive carriers of culture.

Erving Goffman gave the tradition its most vivid empirical form. The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, of 1959, analysed interaction dramaturgically, with front and back regions, performance, impression management and face-work. Asylums, of 1961, examined the total institution and the systematic mortification of the self it performs on inmates. Stigma, of 1963, analysed spoiled identity. Frame Analysis, of 1974, asked how people answer the question of what is going on here, and showed how much interpretive work is needed before any situation can be acted in at all.

sections.heading: Ethnomethodology and the Breaching Experiment
sections.body:
Harold Garfinkel's Studies in Ethnomethodology, published in 1967, pushed the analysis to its most radical point by asking not what social order is but how, moment to moment, people produce it. Ethnomethodology means the study of the methods ordinary members use to make their activities accountable — that is, observable, reportable and recognisable as the ordinary activities they are. Garfinkel's target was the assumption that social order is a thing lying behind conduct. On his account it is an ongoing accomplishment, produced continuously and locally, and it exists nowhere but in that production.

Three concepts carry the argument. Indexicality is the observation that the meaning of any utterance depends irreducibly on its context: the same words mean different things said by different people at different times, and no amount of specification eliminates this, because every clarification is itself indexical. Reflexivity is the observation that descriptions of a situation are part of that situation and help constitute it; a chairperson announcing that the meeting has begun does not report a fact but creates one. Accountability is the observation that people design their actions so as to be recognisable as what they are, which is why activities can be followed at all.

Garfinkel demonstrated the invisible labour involved through breaching experiments, in which students disrupted a taken-for-granted expectation and observed the reaction. Asked how they were, they demanded to know in what respect. In their own homes they behaved as polite lodgers, asking permission to use the bathroom. Playing noughts and crosses, they erased an opponent's mark and moved it. The findings were consistent and striking: not confusion but rapid, intense moral indignation. Subjects did not treat the breach as a puzzle to be solved but as an offence requiring an account, and relationships were sometimes genuinely damaged. The background expectancies of everyday life turn out to be moral obligations, defended as such.

Garfinkel's best-known case study concerned a person he called Agnes, a young transgender woman he studied from 1958 with Robert Stoller. Agnes had to accomplish continuously, and under threat of exposure, what others achieved without noticing: being recognised as a woman in every setting, with the right knowledge, the right biography and the right competences. The case made visible that gender for everyone is an ongoing practical achievement, not a passive attribute — an insight that Candace West and Don Zimmerman developed in their much-cited 1987 paper on doing gender.

Ethnomethodology has been criticised for indifference to power, history and inequality, and for a prose style that is genuinely difficult. Its contribution is nonetheless distinctive. Where other approaches treat social structure as a background explaining behaviour, ethnomethodology insists that structure has no existence apart from the countless local practices that reproduce it.

sections.heading: Foucault: Discourse, Power and Historical Categories
sections.body:
Michel Foucault rarely used the vocabulary of social construction and would have resisted it, but his historical work supplied constructionism with much of its evidence and nearly all of its account of power. His method was to take a category that seems timelessly natural — madness, illness, criminality, sexuality — and to reconstruct the historically specific conditions under which it became thinkable, sayable and administrable.

The History of Madness, of 1961, traced how the mad, previously integrated in various ways into European communities, were caught up in what Foucault called the great confinement of the seventeenth century, institutionalised alongside the poor and the idle, and only later constituted as objects of a specifically medical knowledge. The Birth of the Clinic, of 1963, examined the emergence around 1800 of the clinical gaze, a way of seeing that located disease in lesions within the body rather than in the patient's narrated experience, thereby producing both a new object of knowledge and a new kind of authority.

The Order of Things, of 1966, introduced the episteme: the underlying configuration of a period that determines what can count as knowledge at all, and which changes not gradually but in ruptures. The Archaeology of Knowledge, of 1969, made the method explicit, analysing discourses as systems that produce their own objects rather than as descriptions of pre-existing ones. Discipline and Punish, of 1975, traced the shift from public torture to the prison and analysed the disciplinary techniques — timetables, examination, hierarchical observation, normalising judgement — that produce docile and useful bodies, taking Jeremy Bentham's panopticon as the emblem of a power that works by the possibility of being seen.

The first volume of The History of Sexuality, of 1976, contains the argument most often cited by constructionists. Against the repressive hypothesis, which holds that the Victorians silenced sex and that modernity is a liberation, Foucault argued that the nineteenth century produced an enormous proliferation of discourse about sex in medicine, psychiatry, law and pedagogy, and that this discourse did not describe pre-existing types of person but produced them. His much-quoted claim is that the sodomite had been a temporary aberration, whereas the homosexual became a species — a personage with a case history, a childhood and a nature — a shift he associated with psychiatric writing around 1870.

Foucault's central conceptual move is power-knowledge: the claim that power and knowledge are not opposed but mutually constituting, since every exercise of power generates knowledge and every body of knowledge creates positions of authority. Power on this account is not primarily repressive but productive; it produces subjects, categories, pleasures and truths. Critics have objected that this makes resistance hard to ground and that Foucault's historical scholarship is sometimes overstated. Even so, his work supplied the field with something Berger and Luckmann lacked: an account of why some constructions prevail over others.

sections.heading: Hacking's Question: The Construction of What?
sections.body:
By the late 1990s the phrase had been applied to so many things — quarks, emotions, danger, illness, authorship, Zulu nationalism, serial homicide — that the philosopher Ian Hacking wrote a book in 1999 asking what the claims had in common. The Social Construction of What? is the most useful piece of housekeeping the field has, because it insists on precision about the object, the point and the strength of any given claim.

Hacking's first move is to notice that construction claims are usually not about objects at all but about classifications, and that the two are constantly conflated. It is not children who are constructed but the classification child abuse, or the category of the hyperactive child. The physical events, bodies and behaviours may be perfectly real and independent of us; what is our doing is the way we carve them up, the significance we attach to the carving, and the institutions we build on it. Keeping this straight dissolves many arguments in which one party defends the reality of the phenomenon while the other attacks the historical contingency of the category.

His second move is to identify the point of such claims. A construction claim about X ordinarily presupposes that X appears inevitable and natural, and asserts that it need not have existed, or need not be as it is. Often it adds that X is bad, and sometimes that we would be better off without X. Hacking arranges the possible commitments on a scale: historical construction, which merely traces origins; ironic, which notes contingency but expects no change; reformist, which wants the thing modified; unmasking, which aims to strip a category of its authority by exposing its function; rebellious; and revolutionary, which actively campaigns to abolish it. Confusion arises when a purely historical claim is read as revolutionary, or the reverse.

His third and most original contribution is the distinction between indifferent and interactive kinds. Quarks are indifferent: they do not know they are classified as quarks and do not change their behaviour on that account. Human kinds are interactive. People classified as refugees, as gifted, as autistic, as obese, become aware of the classification, and it changes how they understand themselves, how they behave, and how institutions treat them — which in turn changes the class of people the classification picks out, which may prompt experts to revise the classification. Hacking calls this the looping effect of human kinds, and set it out in his 1986 essay Making Up People.

The looping effect explains why some categories in the human sciences behave so unlike categories in chemistry. It also grounds Hacking's studies of transient mental illnesses in Rewriting the Soul, of 1995, on multiple personality, and Mad Travellers, of 1998, on the fugue epidemic of the 1880s: diagnoses that flourish in a particular ecological niche of medical taxonomy, cultural polarity and observability, and fade when the niche closes.

sections.heading: Case Study: Race
sections.body:
Race is the case where constructionist analysis is most firmly established empirically, and also where the claim is most often misheard. The scientific consensus across biological anthropology and genetics is that the folk racial categories used in modern societies do not correspond to discrete, biologically bounded human subspecies. The American Anthropological Association's 1998 Statement on Race put the position formally, and it is worth being clear about the evidence rather than asserting it.

Human genetic variation is overwhelmingly continuous and clinal, changing gradually with geography rather than jumping at boundaries, because populations have exchanged genes continuously. In a much-cited 1972 analysis, Richard Lewontin partitioned variation at seventeen polymorphic loci and found that roughly 85 per cent lay within local populations, about 8 per cent between populations within a conventional race, and only about 6 per cent between the races themselves. Later work with far more markers has broadly confirmed the apportionment. It has, however, also produced a genuine qualification: A. W. F. Edwards argued in 2003 that Lewontin's inference was too quick, since correlations across many loci simultaneously do allow individuals to be assigned to geographic ancestry clusters with high accuracy. The honest summary is that continental ancestry is statistically detectable, that ancestry clusters do not match folk racial categories in their boundaries or their content, and that the variation is nested and gradual rather than typological.

The historical evidence is at least as strong. Racial categories differ across societies and change over time in ways that biology cannot explain. The United States operated a rule of hypodescent, the so-called one-drop rule, under which any known African ancestry made a person Black; Brazil developed a large, fluid vocabulary of colour terms in which siblings can be classified differently and classification shifts with wealth and context. United States census categories have been repeatedly redrawn, with groups added, merged and abolished. Groups now unproblematically counted as white in Britain and America, including Irish, Italian and Jewish populations, were at various points treated as racially distinct.

None of this makes race unreal. This is the point most often lost. Race is a social fact with enormous causal power: it structures wealth, housing, policing, health outcomes and life expectancy, and those effects are measurable in the same way as any others. Racism is not diminished by the finding that its object is a construction; if anything the finding sharpens the question of how the construction came to be built and whose interests it served. The historical answer generally offered is that modern racial categories were consolidated in the era of Atlantic slavery and European colonial expansion, as a justification for a hierarchy that already existed economically, rather than as a discovery that preceded it.

sections.heading: Case Study: Sex, Gender and Performativity
sections.body:
The sex-gender distinction is the most widely known application of constructionist thinking and also the most politically charged, so it is worth setting out carefully what the various claims are and where genuine disagreement lies.

The founding statement is Simone de Beauvoir's in The Second Sex of 1949: one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. Her argument was that the social meaning of femininity is not deducible from female biology but is produced through upbringing, expectation, myth and constraint, and that woman had been constituted as the Other against a male norm treated as simply human. In Anglophone social science the distinction was formalised in the 1970s, notably in Ann Oakley's Sex, Gender and Society of 1972, which used sex for biological characteristics and gender for the social roles, behaviours and expectations attached to them. On this weaker and now widely accepted view, the enormous cross-cultural and historical variation in what men and women are supposed to do, wear, feel and be good at is evidence that these are cultural rather than biological products.

The evidence for that weaker claim is substantial. Occupations coded as male in one society are coded as female in another; clothing, colour conventions, expressiveness norms and inheritance rules vary dramatically; and the demonstrated capacities of women and men change rapidly when institutional barriers are removed, which is not what one expects from a fixed biological cause. Anthropologists have also documented societies with recognised social categories beyond a binary, including the hijra in South Asia, and various third-gender roles in Indigenous North American and Polynesian societies, though these are not equivalent to modern Western identity categories and should not be flattened into them.

The stronger and more contested claim concerns whether the underlying category of sex is itself constructed. Judith Butler's Gender Trouble of 1990 argued that gender is performative — not a role played by a pre-existing self but a stylised repetition of acts through which the appearance of an inner gendered essence is produced — and that the sex-gender distinction covertly smuggles in the naturalness of sex. Butler's Bodies That Matter of 1993 responded to the charge that this denies material bodies, arguing instead that bodies are never encountered outside the categories through which they are made intelligible.

This is where genuine and unresolved disagreement sits. Critics hold that reproductive biology is a brute fact with real consequences and that constructionist analysis overreaches when applied to it. Defenders hold that the criteria used to sort bodies into two sexes — chromosomes, gonads, hormones, genitalia, secondary characteristics — do not always align, that intersex variation is a real if uncommon phenomenon, and that the decision to treat the categories as exhaustive is itself a choice. A reader should know that this is a live argument in which reasonable scholars differ, not a settled question.

sections.heading: Case Study: Mental Illness and Diagnostic Categories
sections.body:
Psychiatric classification is the domain where constructionist analysis has been most useful and most easily abused, and where the distinction between the category and the suffering it names has to be held with particular care.

The historical evidence that diagnostic categories are made rather than found is not seriously disputed. Samuel Cartwright, a Louisiana physician, proposed in 1851 a disorder he called drapetomania, whose symptom was the tendency of enslaved people to run away — a category that told you a great deal about the society that produced it and nothing about the people it labelled. Neurasthenia was among the most common diagnoses in the late nineteenth century and has effectively disappeared. Hysteria, an anchor of nineteenth-century psychiatry, was removed from the American classification in 1980 and dispersed among other categories. Homosexuality was listed as a mental disorder in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual until the American Psychiatric Association voted to remove it in December 1973, a change reflected in printings from 1974, and it was replaced for a period by the narrower category of ego-dystonic homosexuality before that too was dropped. That a diagnosis can be settled by a professional vote is not, by itself, evidence that it was wrong, but it does make the social process visible in an unusually direct way.

Structural changes matter as much as individual entries. The third edition of the manual, published in 1980 under Robert Spitzer, replaced the previous psychoanalytically inflected descriptions with explicit operational criteria — checklists with thresholds and durations. This vastly improved diagnostic reliability, meaning that two clinicians would more often agree, but reliability is not validity, and the criteria and thresholds themselves were the product of committee decisions, clinical judgement and negotiation, subsequently entrenched by insurance systems, drug regulation and research funding that all require a diagnostic code.

Ian Hacking's looping effect is especially visible here. When a diagnosis becomes available, people encounter it, recognise themselves in it, and reorganise their self-understanding and behaviour around it; clinicians look for it and find it; the population picked out by the category shifts; and the category is revised in response. Hacking's studies of the nineteenth-century fugue epidemic and of the rise and fall of multiple personality diagnoses in North America trace this process in detail, arguing that such conditions flourish in a temporary ecological niche and recede when it closes.

The essential caution is that none of this shows the distress is unreal or that treatment is illegitimate. The anti-psychiatry writing of the 1960s, particularly Thomas Szasz's claim that mental illness is a myth, took the argument further than the evidence supports and had real costs. The defensible position is that severe psychiatric suffering is entirely real, that its classification is a historically contingent human artefact, and that both facts must be held at once.

sections.heading: Constructionism About Science, and the Science Wars
sections.body:
The most contentious extension of the programme was to natural science itself. If knowledge in general is socially produced, does that include physics? The sociology of scientific knowledge, developed in Britain from the mid-1970s, said yes, and the resulting argument became bitter enough to be called the science wars.

The programmatic statement is David Bloor's Knowledge and Social Imagery of 1976, which set out the strong programme in four tenets. Explanations of belief should be causal. They should be impartial between true and false beliefs, both requiring explanation. They should be symmetrical, using the same kinds of cause to explain both. And they should be reflexive, applying to sociology itself. The symmetry principle was the flashpoint: earlier sociology had explained error socially while explaining truth by reason and evidence, and Bloor argued that this exempted the interesting cases from analysis.

Empirical laboratory studies followed. Bruno Latour and Steve Woolgar's Laboratory Life, published in 1979 with the subtitle The Social Construction of Scientific Facts, treated a neuroendocrinology laboratory anthropologically and described how statements move from being hedged claims to unqualified facts as the traces of their production are stripped away. In a detail that says much about the field's own second thoughts, the 1986 edition dropped the word Social from the subtitle. Harry Collins identified the experimenter's regress: to know whether an experiment was competently performed you need to know what the correct result is, but that is what the experiment was supposed to determine, so closure must come from something beyond the data alone.

The reaction was fierce. Paul Gross and Norman Levitt's Higher Superstition of 1994 accused the field of ignorance and hostility toward science. In 1996 the physicist Alan Sokal submitted a deliberately meaningless article to the cultural studies journal Social Text, which published it, and then revealed the hoax. The episode was widely read as an indictment of the field's standards, though it demonstrated a failure of editorial review at one non-peer-reviewed journal rather than refuting any particular thesis.

Two decades on, a moderate settlement is discernible. Almost everyone now accepts that scientific practice is a social activity, that funding, careers, instruments, institutions and rhetoric shape which questions get asked and which results get accepted, and that this is a legitimate and productive object of study. Far fewer accept the strong claim that the content of well-confirmed physical theory is determined by social factors rather than by the world. The obvious retort — that aeroplanes fly and vaccines work whoever built the institutions — is not a knockdown argument, since sophisticated versions accommodate it, but it marks where most working scientists and many philosophers draw the line.

sections.heading: The Serious Objections
sections.body:
A position worth holding should be able to state the strongest case against it. Several objections to constructionism are serious, and some versions of the position do not survive them.

The first is self-refutation. If all knowledge is socially constructed and none tracks a mind-independent reality, then that claim is itself socially constructed and has no better standing than its denial. This is the ancient objection to relativism, made against Protagoras by Plato in the Theaetetus, and it bites hard against the strongest formulations. Sophisticated constructionists answer that recognising the social conditions of knowledge production does not entail that all beliefs are equally warranted, and Bloor's reflexivity tenet accepts the application to sociology without conceding incoherence. Whether that answer is adequate is genuinely debated; Paul Boghossian's Fear of Knowledge of 2006 argues at length that it is not.

The second is the conflation objection, which Ian Hacking pressed from inside the field: construction claims slide between the classification and the thing classified. The category of quark is unquestionably a human artefact with a history; whether quarks are is a completely different question, and eliding the two produces claims that sound radical and turn out either trivial or false.

The third is the triviality objection. If the claim is only that concepts are human products expressed in human languages, everyone agrees and nothing has been shown. For the claim to be substantive it must assert something specific: that the thing could not exist without our practices, or that the classification is historically contingent in a way that undermines its authority, or that it is sustained by an interest that would not survive being made explicit. Each of these requires argument and evidence about the particular case.

The fourth is the neglect of material and biological constraint. Constructions are not made from nothing. Bodies age and die, crops fail in drought, viruses transmit, materials have tensile strengths. A theory that cannot say why some constructions succeed and others collapse has not explained much, and the better work — including Searle's insistence on a brute-fact background — takes this seriously.

The fifth is a political objection made from both directions. Some argue that showing a category to be constructed does not by itself show it to be bad, since money, marriage and law are constructed and mostly useful; the leap from contingency to critique requires an independent moral argument that is often left implicit. Others argue the opposite, that constructionist analysis dissolves the shared factual ground on which political argument depends, and that its tools are as available to those denying well-evidenced findings as to critics of injustice. Both worries have force, and the honest response is that the analysis is a descriptive instrument, not a politics.

sections.heading: Using the Idea Well
sections.body:
The practical value of constructionism lies in the questions it teaches you to ask, and those questions can be stated without any theoretical vocabulary at all. Faced with any category that presents itself as simply how things are, ask when it appeared, since a category with a datable origin is not a fact of nature. Ask what it replaced, since the previous arrangement shows the alternatives. Ask who does the classifying and with what authority. Ask what institutional consequences follow from being placed in one box rather than another — money, liberty, medical treatment, legal standing. Ask whose interests the arrangement serves, without assuming that the answer is the whole explanation. Ask whether the classification changes the people classified, which is the looping effect and the mark of a genuinely social kind. And ask what would have to change for the category to lose its grip.

Equally important is knowing when the analysis does not apply, or applies only weakly. Several tests help. Does the thing behave the same way regardless of what anyone believes about it, across cultures with no contact? Does it have effects that no institution sustains? Would it persist if every human died? Radioactive decay passes all three; a credit rating passes none. Most interesting cases are mixed: tuberculosis is caused by a bacillus that does not care what we call it, while the category of the consumptive, the moral meanings attached to the disease, the social distribution of exposure and the priority given to treating it are all thoroughly social. The mature position is not to sort things into constructed and real but to specify which aspects of a phenomenon depend on us and which do not.

Three habits guard against the common abuses. First, always say what is supposed to be constructed — the object, the category, the meaning, the institution, or the causal claim about it — because most bad arguments come from leaving this vague. Second, keep the descriptive claim separate from the evaluative one; showing that something was made does not show it was made badly, and showing that a category has an ugly history does not show that everything within it is worthless. Third, resist the inference from constructed to easily changed. Constructions are held in place by law, habit, socialisation, infrastructure and the coordinated expectations of millions of people, which is why they are difficult to shift and why understanding their machinery is a precondition of changing them.

Used this way the idea is neither a cynical solvent nor a slogan. It is a method for recovering the human authorship of arrangements that present themselves as necessary, so that they can be examined, defended on their merits, or deliberately rebuilt.

guides.title: Functionalism, Conflict Theory & Symbolic Interactionism
guides.summary: A guided tour of sociology's three major theoretical paradigms: their origins, key thinkers, core concepts, how each explains the same social facts differently, and the criticisms and syntheses that shape the discipline today.

sections.heading: Why Sociology Has Competing Paradigms
sections.body: Sociology, unlike the natural sciences, is a multi-paradigm discipline: it contains several distinct theoretical frameworks that coexist rather than one that has defeated the others. A paradigm, in Thomas Kuhn's sense, is a shared set of assumptions, concepts, questions, and methods that guides a community of researchers. Kuhn argued that mature natural sciences work within a single reigning paradigm punctuated by rare revolutions; sociology instead operates permanently with three or four rival frameworks, each with its own vision of what society is and how it should be studied. The three that anchor most introductory treatments are structural functionalism, conflict theory, and symbolic interactionism. They differ along two great axes. The first is the level of analysis. Functionalism and conflict theory are macro-level, or macrosociological, theories: they look at large-scale structures such as institutions, classes, and whole societies, treating individuals as occupants of positions within systems. Symbolic interactionism is micro-level, or microsociological: it looks at face-to-face interaction, at how meaning is made in the small encounters of daily life. The second axis concerns the fundamental character of social order. Functionalism sees society as basically integrated and cooperative, held together by consensus over shared values; conflict theory sees it as basically divided and coercive, held together by the domination of some groups over others; symbolic interactionism largely brackets that grand question to examine how order is accomplished moment by moment through shared symbols. Each paradigm therefore asks different questions and notices different facts. Confronted with the family, functionalism asks what needs the family meets for society, conflict theory asks whose interests the family serves and what inequalities it reproduces, and interactionism asks how people negotiate the meaning of being a spouse or parent in everyday interaction. None of these is simply right or wrong; they are lenses, and each illuminates what the others obscure. This is why sociologists speak of theoretical pluralism as a strength rather than an embarrassment: a rich account of any social phenomenon usually needs more than one. It also means students must learn to hold several frameworks at once and to ask, of any social pattern, what each paradigm would make of it. The chapters that follow trace the origins of these three traditions, unfold their central concepts and leading thinkers, show how they analyse the same facts differently, and confront the criticisms each has drawn. A fourth framework, feminist theory, is sometimes counted as a paradigm in its own right and is treated here mainly within the conflict tradition it extends. The aim throughout is not to crown a winner but to equip the reader to think sociologically from more than one angle, which is the discipline's distinctive habit of mind.

sections.heading: Roots: The Organic Analogy and the Birth of Social Theory
sections.body: The three paradigms did not appear fully formed; they grew from nineteenth-century attempts to make society an object of scientific study. The word sociology was coined by the French philosopher Auguste Comte in the 1830s, and Comte set the ambition that would shape functionalism. He proposed a positivist science of society modelled on the natural sciences, dividing the field into social statics, the study of order and the forces that hold society together, and social dynamics, the study of change and progress. Comte also introduced the organic analogy, the comparison of society to a living body, that recurs throughout functionalist thought. The English philosopher Herbert Spencer developed the analogy systematically in the second half of the century. Society, he argued, is like an organism: it grows, becomes more complex and differentiated as it grows, develops specialised organs, or institutions, that perform distinct functions, and depends on the coordination of those parts for its survival. Spencer distinguished the regulatory, sustaining, and distributive systems of society by analogy with the nervous, digestive, and circulatory systems of the body. He is often associated with social Darwinism and the phrase survival of the fittest, which he coined, though his evolutionary optimism about laissez-faire progress is now largely discredited. What survived from Comte and Spencer was the core functionalist intuition that a society is a system of interdependent parts and that each recurring feature can be understood by the contribution it makes to the whole. Against this current, the German philosopher and revolutionary Karl Marx was building the intellectual foundations of conflict theory, though he never called himself a sociologist. Writing on the industrial capitalism transforming Europe, Marx insisted that the driving force of history was not consensus but struggle between classes with irreconcilable material interests. His materialist theory of history and his analysis of exploitation would be developed into the conflict paradigm generations later. The micro tradition had different roots, in the German thinker Georg Simmel, who studied the forms of social interaction, association, and the effects of group size, and in American pragmatist philosophy, especially the work of William James, Charles Sanders Peirce, and John Dewey, which held that meaning arises through practical action and that the mind and self are social products. These three streams, the organicism of Comte and Spencer, the class analysis of Marx, and the interactional and pragmatist concern with meaning, flowed into the three classical figures who founded modern sociological theory proper, Emile Durkheim, Karl Marx as read by later theorists, and Max Weber, and from them into the paradigms that structure the discipline today. Understanding this genealogy shows that the paradigms are not arbitrary; each is a disciplined development of a real and enduring insight about social life.

sections.heading: Functionalism: Durkheim, Solidarity, and Social Facts
sections.body: Emile Durkheim, working in France around the turn of the twentieth century, gave functionalism its classical form and made sociology an academic discipline. His first methodological rule, stated in The Rules of Sociological Method of 1895, was to treat social facts as things. A social fact is a way of acting, thinking, or feeling that is general throughout a society, external to any individual, and exercising a constraint on him; law, morality, religion, language, and currency are examples.
